title: UPDATE: Zero-Order Training Hits New FineWeb-30M Record With 7.9 Minute Run
summary:
Robert Lange reached a validation loss of 3.5 on the FineWeb-30M zero-order optimization benchmark in 7.9 minutes using a single 8xH100 node. The training run, which occurred without backpropagation, is a 12.9x improvement over the previous record of 102.5 minutes set by the Noise speedrun.

The speedup was achieved using CUDA graphs, fused kernels, and a revised Cut estimator to reduce probe costs. This follows other recent breakthroughs in zeroth-order optimization, including the Dust algorithm's efficiency in models up to 243M parameters and community methods that reached a validation loss of 3.409 on the 30M token track, beating the 3.419 loss of the standard backprop and Adam approach.

selectedTweets.text:
First record on the new zero-order optimization benchmark FineWeb-30M speedrun track: 

val loss 3.5 with no backprop in 7.9 min on one 8×H100 node, down from Noise's 102.5 min (×12.9). Here is a breakdown of internal stepping stone records:

🟠 102.5 min: Noise's record. Their Boost → Cut estimator from the 10M track, run over the full 30M epoch. It ends at 3.41, far below the 3.5 target, so there was margin to spend.

🟢 35.6 min (×2.9): identity path first, then Cut. We first spent the margin on fewer rows and added tiled probe kernels. Then came the bigger structural change: one phase trains the first ~6k rows with our 10M-speedrun identity-path trainer in 3.5 s, then hands the weights to Cut for the rest. That removes the Boost phase and Cut's most expensive probes. Cheap training does the early, easy part; the careful estimator does the rest.

🟣 12.9 min (×8.0): 8 rows per update. On the way: a leaner Cut (fewer probe types, half the keys and MLP routes) and bf16 activations in the reruns. Then each GPU got its own sequence, which removes the work paired GPUs used to duplicate (−13% per row). It also halves the estimator's noise, so the best learning rate goes back up.

🔵 7.9 min (×12.9): the math and systems tail. The readout's change now comes from second-order moments instead of the full 4,096-token vocab, the moved queries run in one fused kernel, the norm's change is folded into the next projection, the end merge runs as a CUDA graph, and the reruns use 1024-token chunks. Each step gives a few percent, with the gradient checked against the previous version before every run.

All of this took about a day of autodiscovery magic. One observation about speedruns as a research tool: Today's runtime gain improves tomorrow's search budget. At 102.5 min per run, one 8×H100 node can test about 14 ideas a day; at 7.9 min it can test about 180. Each faster record makes the next round of experiments cheaper, so the same compute buys many more hypotheses, including riskier ones you'd never spend a 2-hour run on.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
I think the last month might have been the biggest month in (zeroth-order) optimization history.

In the 10 days since we released the Noise speedrun, the time to pretrain a transformer went from 1.76 hours to 1.6 seconds, a 4,000x (!!!) speedup. Dust itself was up to 10,000x more compute-efficient than the previous state-of-the-art.

Not only can we pretrain a transformer without backprop, it's much more efficient than anyone would've expected. Search fking works!

Now, scaling is the biggest open question. Some of the tricks that brought the time down to 1.6 seconds will simply not scale. To discard those, we'll be scaling the dataset every time it gets overfit, starting with 30M tokens instead of 10M.

Huge thanks to @jayden_teoh_, @spicey_lemonade, @RobertTLange, @EmanueleRodola, @ChunyuanDeng, @LuochengHuman, @Alaxarr, @pavleculafic, @IsaacYong13, Euraba and areu01or00 (GitHub), for the contributions. And @cs_serdar for gracefully maintaining the speedrun and @bishmdl76 for helping out.

Expect a lot more from us over the coming weeks.

selectedTweets.bestBit: making ZO work at scale requires changing the architecture to think in ensembles vs one giant monolith
selectedTweets.text:
for everyone new to zero order, zoo is the future and has amazing properties over BP. 

but requires a change in architecture as there is no "gradient flow" you need to worry about. you just jump. rendering most previous architectures over engineered and previous mental models unhelpful. 

but the issue w ZO will always be dimensionality that you cant solve wo changing the architecture. i tried the last 2 years wo much success on anything except fine tuning. could never pretrain. 

here is the key issue: 
if you want to train an 8B parameter model, over lets say 100k steps, w 64 perturbations, then you have only ever checked 6 million halfspaces, less than 0.1%. so 99.9% of the directions in the model have never been explored ever. thus the gradient noise is way too high esp at later stages of training. 

initial training will look good, bc initially, all directions give finite differences in loss. but later training stalls abruptly, bc in late training almost all directions are degenerate so every probe produces near 0 finite difference. (this is also why speedrunning zoo is not a good idea.. wont tell you much..)

but split those 8B parameters into independently trained 10K experts, SOMA-style, and w just 10 perturbations per step for 1K steps, each expert gets 10k probes, enough for those directions to span all directions in design space. finite differences remain high always. 

estimating a useful update in 10K dimensions isnt too hard and even better each expert training is independent loop, so no comms btwn gpus! 

this enables pretraining at scale w zoo. and nothing else does. not hyperbole. ive trained everything else. you need to shard the model. 

this is how the brain is organized too btw. all sensory information is sent to the thalamus (except olfactory) which routes those signals to tiny cortical columns in your neocortex that are massively inhibited and train independently from each other and we ensemble the results at test time. 

TLDR: making ZO work at scale requires changing the architecture to think in ensembles vs one giant monolith. Also worth mentioning, even better if you have a chip that is optimized for fpasses (eg etched/tpu_i/photonics/neuromorphics) not gpus.

selectedTweets.bestBit: As the cost of hill climbing goes down, exploring a new idea can become much cheaper
selectedTweets.text:
Interesting that automated hill climbing might end up encouraging fundamental innovation.

As the cost of hill climbing goes down, exploring a new idea can become much cheaper.
Historically, exploring a new direction could require a prohibitively large investment in optimizing everything to match the performance of a mature method, especially when other layers have been co-optimized for that mature method.
